item.title: 1950: White Sox Release Luke Appling, 43, After 21 Seasons
item.description: After 2,422 games played (and 2,749 career hits) over his 21-season career, the Chicago White Sox release veteran Luke Appling, 43, their long-time shortstop and two-time American League batting champion. "Ol' Aches and Pains" will be elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1964, and the White Sox will eventually retire Appling's #4 uniform. Photo: Unknown (Public domain).

item.title: 2023: Clubs Face Deadline to Make Qualifying Offers to Free Agents
item.description: Deadline for clubs to make qualifying offers to their eligible players who become free agents.

item.title: 2021: Travelers Name Her Permanent GM, First Woman in Franchise History
item.description: On November 9, 2021, the Travelers named her the permanent general manager, making her the first woman to hold the position in franchise history.

item.title: 2018: Joe Mauer Retires, Announces Decision in Open Letter to Fans
item.description: On November 9, 2018, Mauer officially retired from baseball in an open letter to Twins fans. Photo: Keith Allison from Hanover, MD, USA (CC BY-SA 2.0).

item.title: 2016: Georgia State, Atlanta Reach Tentative Deal for Turner Field
item.description: On August 18, 2016, Georgia State and the Atlanta-Fulton County Recreation Authority reached a tentative purchase agreement for Turner Field, and the purchase and redevelopment plan was approved by the Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia on November 9, 2016. Photo: RyanW20.01 (CC BY-SA 4.0).

item.title: 2012: Lee MacPhail, 95, Former AL President and Team Executive
item.description: Lee MacPhail, 95, American League president from 1974 to 1983, and longtime team executive (New York Yankees, Baltimore Orioles); oldest living Hall of Fame member, and part of the only father-son duo in the Hall (with his father, Larry MacPhail, who introduced night games to the majors in 1935); father of longtime executive Andy MacPhail.

item.title: 2011: Nationals Catcher Wilson Ramos Kidnapped at Mother's Home
item.description: Washington Nationals catcher Wilson Ramos is kidnapped by four gunmen from the front yard of his mother's home in Valencia in his native Venezuela. He is rescued by Venezuelan authorities on November 11 during an air operation in the mountains in the state of Carabobo, roughly 40 miles northwest of where he is abducted. Photo: MissChatter on Flickr (Original version) UCinternational (Crop) (CC BY 2.0).

item.title: 2008: Saitama Seibu Lions Beat Yomiuri Giants 3-2, Win Japan Series
item.description: The Saitama Seibu Lions beat the Yomiuri Giants 3–2 in Game 7 in the Japan Series, winning the series 4–3. Photo: Rikigon (CC BY-SA 3.0).

item.title: 2007: Italy Beats Team USA, Handing Its Only Loss in World Cup Run
item.description: Italy handed the U.S. team their only loss in Team USA's route to win the 2007 Baseball World Cup in Taiwan. It was the U.S.'s first loss to Italy in 21 years and the first time it ever lost to Italy with professional players, as the team consisted of Major League Baseball players and top minor league prospects. Photo: Ludahai (CC BY-SA 4.0).

item.title: 2006: Taichung Stadium Opens, Replacing Antiquated Taichung Baseball Field
item.description: The stadium officially opened on November 9, 2006, replacing the antiquated Taichung Baseball Field. Photo: No machine-readable author provided. Ludahai assumed (based on (Public domain).

item.title: 2005: Bush Awards Robinson Presidential Medal of Freedom
item.description: Bush awarded Robinson the Presidential Medal of Freedom on November 9, 2005. Photo: Unknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 2004: Clemens, 42, Wins 7th Cy Young, First in National League
item.description: Roger Clemens of the Houston Astros grabbed his 7th Cy Young Award, but the first in the National League. At age 42, he won 18 games and struck out 218 batters.

item.title: 1995: Nomo Named NL Rookie of Year, First Japanese Winner
item.description: Los Angeles Dodgers pitcher Hideo Nomo is named National League Rookie of the Year, becoming the first Japanese player ever to win a Major League award. Nomo posts a 13-6 record with 236 strikeouts and a 2.54 ERA in 191 1/3 innings of work.

item.title: 1988: Bob Weiland, 82, Left-Hander for Five Clubs
item.description: Bob Weiland, 82, left-hander who went 62–94 (4.24) in 277 games in a dozen seasons (1928–1935, 1937–1940) for five clubs, primarily the St. Louis Cardinals and Boston Red Sox.

item.title: 1982: Yount Named AL MVP After .318 Season for Brewers
item.description: Robin Yount of the Milwaukee Brewers is named American League MVP. During the Brewers' AL-pennant-winning season season, he batted .318 with 21 home runs, 103 RBIS and 19 steals. Photo: Unknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 1976: Athletics Release Billy Williams, Who Ends With 426 Homers
item.description: The Oakland Athletics release Billy Williams, ending his career with 2,711 hits, 426 home runs, 1,475 RBI and a .290 average.

item.title: 1973: Padres Trade Kirby to Reds for Tolan, Tomlin
item.description: Still poised for a sale and transfer to Washington, D.C., the Padres continue to acquire veteran position players, trading pitcher Clay Kirby to the Cincinnati Reds for centerfielder Bobby Tolan and left-handed relief pitcher Dave Tomlin.

item.title: 1971: Indians Promote Ken Aspromonte, 40, to Manager
item.description: The Cleveland Indians, who finished last in the AL East and lost 102 games in 1971, promote former infielder Ken Aspromonte to manager. Aspromonte, 40, spent the past two seasons at the helm of Triple-A Wichita.

item.title: 1964: Dean Chance, 23, Wins Cy Young With 17 First-Place Votes
item.description: Dean Chance, 23-year-old Los Angeles Angels right-hander, is selected the ninth winner of the Cy Young Award, taking 17 of 20 first-place votes; Larry Jackson (two votes) and Sandy Koufax (one) are distant contenders. In 1964, Chance led the American League in games won (21), earned run average (1.65), complete games (15), shutouts (11), and innings pitched (278<small>1/3</small>); he even earned four saves. Photo: Unknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 1962: Cubs Keep College of Coaches, Drop Charlie Metro
item.description: Chicago Cubs owner Philip K. Wrigley announces that the "College of Coaches" concept will be retained for 1963 but that Charlie Metro, who compiled a 43–69 mark as head coach from June 5 through season's end, will not return. The 1962 Cubs (59–103 overall) finished ninth in the new, ten-team National League, behind the expansion Houston Colt .45s.

item.title: 1960: Roger Maris Edges Mantle to Win AL MVP
item.description: Roger Maris, in his first season as a member of the New York Yankees, edges superstar teammate Mickey Mantle to win the 1960 AL Most Valuable Player Award. Mantle receives more first-place votes (ten) but fewer total points (222) than Maris (eight first-place mentions and 225 points). Brooks Robinson, 23, places third with 211 points and three first-place votes. Photo: Unknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 1953: Supreme Court Rules 7-2 Baseball Is a Sport, Not Business
item.description: Reaffirming its earlier position, the United States Supreme Court rules, 7–2, that baseball is a sport and not a business and therefore not subject to antitrust laws. The ruling is made in a case involving New York Yankees minor league player George Toolson, who refused to move from Triple-A to Double-A.

item.title: 1940: Delaware Beats Pennsylvania Military College 14-7 in First Game
item.description: Delaware played its first game at Wilmington Park on November 9, 1940, and beat Pennsylvania Military College 14–7. Photo: Boston Public Library (Public domain).

item.title: 1937: Cardinals' Joe Medwick Named NL Most Valuable Player
item.description: St. Louis Cardinals Triple Crown winner Joe Medwick is named National League Most Valuable Player by the Baseball Writers' Association of America. Photo: St Louis Cardinals / MLB (Public domain).
